entries.title: Chat can check what a cited paper says
entries.body: On your own articles, pointing at a citation in the text offers a “Does it say that?” button, which opens a new chat asking whether the cited work really says what the paragraph cites it for. To answer, chat can find a copy of the paper that is free to read online, read the passages nearest the claim, and say plainly when it could not get the paper. You can ask for this in any chat about the article too.

entries.title: Chat shows search results inside the conversation
entries.body: When Chat offers to search the article, pressing the button lists the matching passages under its answer, in article order, with a link to the full Search view. It used to take you out of the conversation. Ask Chat for links into the article and it offers passages from the piece, rather than saying it cannot search.

entries.title: Asking about a citation starts from the article
entries.body: Ask in chat about a cited work and the new conversation starts from the article: what point does it use the work to make, and does the work support that? Chat sees the sentences where the article cites it, and is asked to say when it cannot check the work. Before, answers tended to be about the work in general.

entries.title: Short dictated commands are no longer thrown away
entries.body: Any recording shorter than two seconds was thrown away as empty, so a one-word command such as “quotes” never arrived; the limit is now 0.6 seconds. In boxes where pressing Stop twice sends, the first press used to change the button before the second landed; now it holds still, and the second press sends once your words arrive.
